Header:
Date: 2026-02-18

Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (HomeTech CTO), Ben Morales (HomeTech ML Eng), Dana Li (HomeTech Platform)

Summary (auto): Redwood Optimize walkthrough — focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache. Walked through examples, cost model, and trade-offs. Some transcription errors present, product names sometimes garbled (e.g., KV -> K V).

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir with Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Lena, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:09] Aisha: Hey Samir, doing good, thanks. Excited to see the Optimize walkthrough.
[00:14] Ben: Morning, yeah, curious about how batching and the prefix cache will help our costs.
[00:20] Lena: Great — we'll run through the key levers: batching, prefix/K V cache, and then show the cost model scenarios. We'll try to keep it pragmatic.
[00:29] Dana: Quick note — we run in AWS us-west-2, most traffic is bursts around product release, p95 latency target is 200 ms for our assistant.
[00:40] Samir: Perfect, that's helpful, and do you have an on-prem or VPC requirement?
[00:44] Aisha: We need VPC for Prod, plus KMS integration for keys. And SOC2 is a must.
[00:51] Lena: Totally supported — Redwood Private can handle VPC + KMS. For this session we'll focus on the runtime optimizations you can apply regardless of deployment.
[01:05] Ben: Our current baseline is a 13B open model hosted on SageMaker endpoints, avg token length per request is around 350 tokens, and about 1.2M tokens/day. We're seeing token costs balloon.
[01:20] Samir: Ok 1.2M/day gives us good numbers to model. We'll show two optimizations: 1) batching to increase GPU utilization and 2) prefix/K V caching for repeated system prompts and context.
[01:34] Lena: I'll share my screen — apologies if the screen share lags.
[01:40] [screen share starts — slides titled "Optimize: batching & KV cache"]
[01:44] Lena: First, batching — continuous batching versus naive request-by-request. For your traffic shape, where you have bursts but also steady baseline, we typically recommend an adaptive batching policy. The goal is to maximize tokens-per-second per GPU while keeping tail latency within the 200 ms SLO.
[02:02] Ben: How does Redwood decide the batch size? Is it time-based or size-based?
[02:07] Lena: Both. We use a hybrid: a target batch size plus a max wait (e.g., 20 ms). If traffic is low, a small batch is used; if high, we grow to fill the GPU. That reduces per-token GPU overhead. Note: if you need strict single-request latencies, we can pin a lower bound.
[02:26] Aisha: What's the typical latency overhead you see when batching?
[02:30] Lena: For typical LLMs, batching adds a small queuing delay — tens of ms — but can reduce GPU compute time per token by 20–45% depending on kernel efficiency. For your average length (350 tokens) we estimate end-to-end p95 might stay under 200 ms with tuned batching, but we need to test with your exact prompts.
[02:49] [02:49] Samir: Next, prefix vs KV cache — quick primer: prefix caching stores full decoder key/values for tokens that are repeated across requests (like system prompts or instruction templates). KV cache is more dynamic, storing conversation-specific KV segments to avoid recomputing previous context.
[03:10] Ben: Slight correction— I thought KV cache was the same as prefix cache?
[03:14] Lena: It's subtle — folks use the terms interchangeably. In our doc we differentiate: "prefix cache" for static prefixes, and "KV cache" for conversational or session-level caches that can be evicted or shared across replicas.
[03:26] Dana: Any concerns with memory footprint? We have r5-ish instances and want to avoid OOM on dedicated pools.
[03:33] Lena: Good call, caching increases memory; we balance by quantized KV storage and TTL-based eviction. Redwood supports quantized KV (int8-ish) which shrinks footprint substantially, and we surface eviction policies in the console.
[03:45] [03:45] Samir: Let's go through a cost model scenario — I'll run through a simplified spreadsheet.
[03:49] Samir: Baseline: 1.2M tokens/day -> ~36M/month. With current hosted model on SageMaker, folks are seeing $X / 1M tokens — for the sake of demo let's say $25 per 1M tokens inference cost vendor-side (note: placeholder). That would be about $900/month. But typically infra overhead and replication push it higher.
[04:12] Ben: Can you show Redwood's numbers?
[04:15] Lena: Sure. With adaptive batching only, we often see a 20–30% reduction in per-token GPU seconds. With prefix caching for static system prompts representing ~30% of token volume, the incremental savings stack. So combined we model 45–60% cost reduction in many enterprise workloads.
[04:36] [04:36] Ben: That's big — is that realistic for our case?
[04:39] Lena: Depends on reuse. If a large fraction of your tokens are repeated prompts or consistent initial context, prefix caching is very effective. In a chat where every user gets the same 120-token system message, that 120 tokens are cached and not re-computed, which saves both compute and memory I/O.
[04:56] Aisha: What's the operational complexity — do we need to rework our prompt flow?
[05:00] Lena: Minimal. You annotate prefixes in the request payload (we have SDK helpers) or use the console to register common prefixes. For KV cache across sessions, we expose a cache key that you can attach to sessions.
[05:12] [05:12] Samir: I'll show two concrete scenarios on the slide: Scenario A: current baseline (no caching, naive batching). Scenario B: optimized (adaptive batching + prefix cache for system + quantized KV for session history).
[05:24] [slide: table with estimated costs — values approximated for demo]
[05:26] Lena: Baseline: $0.90 per 1k requests (placeholder), Optimized: $0.42 per 1k requests — roughly 53% savings in token compute. Important caveat: network, storage, and control-plane fees vary. This is compute-only.
[05:42] Ben: The slide says quantized KV — how much does quantization affect quality?
[05:46] Lena: We've observed negligible impact for int8 quantized KV on most decoder-only models for retrieval of past tokens. We'll run your evals though. If you need absolute parity we can keep float16 for recent history and quantize older frames.
[05:58] Dana: Regarding fallbacks — if cache miss or eviction occurs, do requests fall back to full compute or degrade gracefully?
[06:04] Lena: Requests fall back to full compute. We also support hybrid fallbacks to cheaper model variants during heavy load — so you can preserve latency SLAs.
[06:14] [06:14] Samir: Security: quick note — for KMS integration we don't store keys, we integrate with customer KMS via envelope encryption. Audit logs are surfaced in the Console and can be forwarded to your SIEM. SOC 2 docs are in the security pack we can share.
[06:27] Aisha: Good. We'll need that for procurement.
[06:31] [06:31] Ben: Can we see a quick demo of registering a prefix and reading cache hit rates?
[06:35] Lena: Sure, switching to the Console demo.
[06:39] [screen shows Redwood Console — Optimize > caching > Prefixes]
[06:43] Lena: Here is the prefixes page: you can add a prefix (name, text blob), select whether it's sharable across customers or org-only, TTL and eviction policy. Once registered, the runtime tags hits and you get hit-rate metrics and cost impact estimates.
[06:57] [07:00] Lena: Example hit rate graph — you can see how during batch processing the hit rate increases and token cost decreases.
[07:08] Ben: If we add prefixes and hit rate is 60% for that 120-token system prompt, that would reduce our 350-token average to what?
[07:15] Lena: Rough calc: if 120 tokens are cached and 60% hit rate, effectively you'd save 0.6 * 120 = 72 tokens per request on average, so new average becomes 278 tokens for compute. Multiplied across your traffic that compounds.
[07:31] Dana: Does Redwood's cost model account for added memory in Dedicated pools? We don't want hidden costs.
[07:37] Samir: We include memory sizing in the dedicated cost estimate. For heavy prefix/KV use you may need larger instances, but the per-token compute savings usually outweigh the slightly higher instance cost. We'll show this in the tailored spreadsheet.
[07:50] [07:50] Ben: About rollout — we'd want to canary prefixes and batching settings. How do you handle rollouts?
[07:56] Lena: In Console we have rollout policies: canary by percentage, A/B split, automatic fallback to baseline if errors or latency breaches thresholds. You can tie rollout to specific model versions too.
[08:09] [08:09] Aisha: Any gotchas with multi-region? We serve users globally.
[08:13] Lena: Smart routing helps — we place caches closer to the serving region. Still, for multi-region low-latency you may want regional replicas of KV cache. That's supported but adds cross-region replication complexity.
[08:24] [08:24] Samir: Let's talk measurement: we'll run a 2-hour benchmark with your sample traces. Lena will set up the job, we collect p50/p95 latency, GPU seconds, and cache hit metrics, then feed into the spreadsheet to produce realistic USD estimates.
[08:40] Ben: Sounds good. For the benchmark, what's the SDK or script you need?
[08:44] Lena: We'll send a curl and python harness. You can also run it from your CI if you prefer. The harness will replay traffic at your observed RPS distribution.
[08:53] [09:00] Samir: A few more Qs from procurement perspective: SLA terms for Dedicated (monthly commit), and data residency options. We'll include contract sketch in the follow-up.
[09:10] Aisha: Procurement will want to see SOC2, encryption at rest, SSO, and audit log retention — please include retention numbers.
[09:18] Samir: Will do. We'll include the security pack and recommended retention settings.
[09:22] [09:22] Ben: One last technical — how do you surface cache hit telemetry? Is it token-level or request-level?
[09:26] Lena: Both. The Console shows aggregated token-level hit rates and request-level hit percentages. You can also stream events to your observability pipeline via our tracing hooks.
[09:37] Dana: If we want to use Redis for session-level KV on-prem, can Redwood integrate?
[09:42] Lena: For Private deployments yes — we can use your Redis cluster as backing store for KV pointers, but we'd still prefer local in-memory caches on the serving nodes for perf. We'll design hybrid approach.
[09:54] [09:54] Samir: Ok wrapping up — recap of agreed next steps and owners.
[09:58] Samir: 1) Samir sends tailored cost model + example numbers by Friday (2026-02-20).
[10:04] Samir: 2) Ben provides 24-hour trace and sample prompts by Monday (2026-02-22).
[10:09] Samir: 3) Lena prepares benchmark playbook and runs 2-hour perf test; target week of 2026-02-24.
[10:16] Aisha: Great, procurement wants SOC2/security docs, so please include.
[10:19] Samir: Yes we'll share the security pack in the doc link after the call.
[10:24] Ben: Quick note — can you include an explicit example of the prefix annotation in our SDK? That would help our engineers.
[10:31] Lena: Absolutely — I'll add snippets for Node/Python.
[10:35] Aisha: Thanks — this was helpful.
[10:37] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule the benchmark.
[10:42] [end of recording]

Notes on transcription errors: some technical terms were auto-transcribed as K V or pre-fix in spots. Speaker overlaps at ~07:00 caused a short timestamp mis-alignment.
